why.correct: The water is the surroundings. When it cools, the process (the system) took energy from it: endothermic. When it warms, the process gave energy to it: exothermic.
options: The water warmed from 21.0 °C to 34.6 °C, so the dissolving released energy into it: exothermic.
The water cooled from 21.0 °C to 11.8 °C: the dissolving drew energy out of the water, so it is endothermic.
The water warmed to 39.2 °C, so the reaction released energy: exothermic.
The water cooled to 16.5 °C: the reaction absorbed energy from the water, so it is endothermic.

why.correct: The water's temperature fell by 9.2 °C, so its particles slowed down: energy left the water and went into the dissolving process.
options: "Cold" is not a thing that moves. Only energy moves, and here it leaves the water.
Right: the dissolving particles absorb energy from the water around them, and the water's temperature drops.
Backward: if the water gained energy, its particles would speed up and its temperature would rise.
The solid was at room temperature. The 9.2 °C drop comes from energy absorbed as the solid dissolves.

why.correct: ΔH is the energy change of the system. The water warmed because the reaction gave it energy, so the reaction lost energy: ΔH is negative.
options: This describes the water, which is the surroundings. ΔH describes the reaction, which lost that energy.
The sign of ΔH follows the system's energy, not the thermometer reading in the surroundings.
Right: energy left the system (the reaction) and entered the surroundings (the water), so ΔH < 0.
The cup keeps energy in the water, but the energy still moved from the reaction to the water.

why.correct: Always ask what is being measured. The thermometer reads the water (surroundings). A warmer surroundings means the system released energy: exothermic.
options: The cup is insulated to keep the room out; the 13.6 °C rise came from the dissolving itself.
The water ended warmer because it received energy; the process that gave the energy is exothermic.
Separating ions does absorb energy, but here more energy is released than absorbed overall, so the water warms.
Right: the classmate described the surroundings. The system, the dissolving, gave energy away.

why.correct: Box 1 is water vapor and Box 2 is liquid water. Hydrogen bonds form between molecules, and forming an attraction releases energy to the surroundings.
options: Right: gas molecules come together into a liquid, and forming hydrogen bonds releases energy.
Box 1 is the gas. Going from Box 1 to Box 2 the molecules come together, which is condensation, not vaporization.
Particles that attract each other release energy as they come together; no input is needed.
Every molecule is still H₂O with the same O–H bonds. Only the attractions between molecules change.

why.correct: Condensation is exothermic, so ΔH < 0 for the water. The energy released comes from the new attractions between molecules; the temperature stays at 100 °C.
options: That is the change from Box 2 to Box 1, where hydrogen bonds must be pulled apart.
Right: forming hydrogen bonds lowers the water's energy, and the difference leaves as energy to the surroundings.
The temperature is constant, but energy still leaves: it comes from the attractions that form, not from slowing the molecules.
The covalent O–H bonds are unchanged. The energy change comes from the attractions between molecules.

why.correct: At constant temperature the kinetic energy of the molecules does not change. The energy comes from potential energy: molecules held by hydrogen bonds sit lower in energy than separated ones.
options: Same temperature means the same average kinetic energy, so the molecules move at the same average speed.
Breaking bonds absorbs energy, and here no covalent bond breaks at all.
Right: molecules held by attractions have lower potential energy, and the difference is released.
The walls do not change; the molecules come together because they attract each other.

why.correct: A process and its reverse have the same size of ΔH with opposite signs. Overcoming the hydrogen bonds absorbs exactly the energy that forming them released.
options: Going backward reverses the direction of the energy: hydrogen bonds are overcome, which absorbs energy.
The temperature stays at 100 °C, so the molecules do not speed up; only the attractions change.
The gas in Box 1 has its molecules separated, the exact reverse of the forward change.
Right: the same attractions that formed must now be overcome, so the same amount of energy goes back in.

why.correct: Exothermic: energy flows out of the system into the surroundings, so the surroundings warm and ΔH is negative.
options: Right: "exo" means out. The system ends with less energy, so ΔH < 0.
That is endothermic: energy goes into the system.
Temperature can change or stay the same either way; what defines the process is the direction of energy.
Many exothermic reactions need a start, and so do some endothermic ones. The start does not set the sign.

why.correct: Processes that form attractions or strong bonds release energy: freezing, condensing and burning. Melting, evaporating and subliming absorb it.
options: Hydrogen bonds form as the molecules lock into place, which releases energy.
Melting overcomes attractions between molecules, which absorbs energy from the counter and air.
Attractions form as the gas becomes liquid, so energy goes into the mirror and it fogs while warming slightly.
Evaporation pulls molecules apart, absorbing energy from your skin; that is why it cools you.
Sublimation separates molecules held by attractions, so it absorbs energy; that is why dry ice chills its surroundings.
Combustion forms strong bonds in CO₂ and H₂O, releasing more energy than it takes to break the reactant bonds.

why.correct: The melting ice is the system and absorbs energy; the surrounding water is the surroundings and gives that energy up, so it cools.

variables.name: Temperature of the liquid water around the ice
variables.why: Energy moves from the warmer water into the ice to melt it, so the water's particles slow down.

variables.name: Energy of the ice as it melts
variables.why: Melting is endothermic: the ice absorbs energy to overcome the hydrogen bonds holding it in place.

variables.name: Total mass of the cup and its contents
variables.why: Melting changes the state of the water, not the amount of matter in the cup.

why.correct: Evaporation is endothermic. The energy needed to separate water molecules comes from the skin, which is the surroundings, so the skin cools.
options: If evaporation released energy to the skin, the skin would warm, not cool.
Sweat leaves the body at body temperature; the cooling comes from the evaporation itself.
The molecules stay intact as H₂O; only the attractions between molecules are overcome.
Right: molecules leaving the liquid must overcome hydrogen bonds, and that energy comes from the skin.

why.correct: Atoms in a bond are attracted to each other, so separating them requires energy. A fuel releases energy because the bonds that form in CO₂ and H₂O release more energy than breaking the fuel's and oxygen's bonds absorbs.
options: Right: atoms in a bond attract each other, so pulling them apart takes energy. The release comes from bond forming.
A high bond energy means more energy is needed to break the bond, not that breaking it releases energy.
Bond breaking takes energy in every substance; the atoms attract each other wherever the bond is.
Bond breaking and forming are where the energy of a reaction comes from.

why.correct: Overall energy released = energy released by forming bonds − energy absorbed by breaking bonds. A hot flask means this is positive, so ΔH is negative.
options: This swaps the two: breaking absorbs energy and forming releases it.
Right: the extra energy left the system and warmed the flask, so the reaction is exothermic.
Then the system would gain energy overall and the flask would cool: endothermic.
The flask got hot because the reaction gave it energy; the reaction rearranged bonds to do so.

why.correct: For the puddle to freeze, energy had to leave it. That energy went into the reacting solids, so the reaction is endothermic and ΔH is positive.
options: "Cold" is not something released. The puddle froze because energy was taken out of it.
If the puddle gained energy, it would warm up and could not freeze.
Right: the puddle lost enough energy to freeze, and that energy went into the reaction, the system.
Water at room temperature does not freeze by itself; the reaction must have removed energy from it.

why.correct: Only a temperature change in the surroundings shows the direction of energy. Water that gets warmer received energy, so the dissolving is exothermic.
options: Dissolving is visible either way; it does not show which way energy moves.
Conductivity shows that ions are present, not which way energy moved.
Mass is conserved in every process, so it says nothing about energy.
Right: the water (surroundings) gained energy from the dissolving (system).

why.correct: Chemists draw the boundary around the reacting particles. The water around them is surroundings, and its temperature change shows the energy the reaction gave or took.
options: Right: the system is the part you study, the reaction, and everything else is surroundings.
The thermometer measures the surroundings. The reaction is what we want to describe.
Then the water's temperature change would be inside the system and would not show energy exchange.
The thermometer is a tool. The thing being studied is the reaction.

why.correct: ΔH is the energy the system gains (positive) or loses (negative) as heat at constant pressure, in J or kJ.
options: Warmer surroundings mean the system released energy, so ΔH is negative.
Right: energy into the system makes ΔH positive (endothermic).
ΔH is an energy, measured in joules or kilojoules, not a temperature.
Energy added to the system makes ΔH positive.

why.correct: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) = 38 kJ − 125 kJ = −87 kJ per mole of reaction. Products sit below reactants, so the sign is negative.
Ea(forward) = H(peak) − H(reactants) = 214 kJ − 125 kJ = 89 kJ/mol.
For the reverse reaction, ΔH = 125 − 38 = +87 kJ/mol and Ea(reverse) = 214 − 38 = 176 kJ/mol. The diagram is read right to left.
options: This copies the forward values. Reversing the direction flips the sign of ΔH and changes which side the climb starts from.
The sign is right, but the reverse climb starts at the products, 38 kJ, not at the reactants.
Right: going backward climbs from 38 kJ to 214 kJ, then ends at 125 kJ, higher than it started.
The reverse reaction passes over the same hump; climbing it from 38 kJ to 214 kJ takes 176 kJ/mol.

why.correct: ΔH depends only on where the reactants and products sit. A catalyst lowers the hump between them.
options: The products are the same substances, so their enthalpy is unchanged.
A catalyst changes the path, which is the peak, not the end points.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy; it does not raise it, and it does not change ΔH.
Right: a catalyst offers a path with a lower activation energy but starts and ends at the same substances.

why.correct: An endothermic reaction ends higher than it starts: products above reactants, ΔH > 0. The height of the hump does not decide this.
options: Products at 110 kJ are above reactants at 50 kJ: ΔH = +60 kJ/mol.
Products at 20 kJ are below reactants at 80 kJ: ΔH = −60 kJ/mol, exothermic.
Products at 95 kJ are above reactants at 30 kJ: ΔH = +65 kJ/mol.
Products at 70 kJ are below reactants at 90 kJ: ΔH = −20 kJ/mol, exothermic.

why.correct: Ea(forward) = top − reactants: P 95, Q 40, R 130, S 60 kJ/mol. The largest is R.
options: P's overall rise is 60 kJ/mol and its climb is 95 kJ/mol; R climbs further.
Right: 160 − 30 = 130 kJ/mol, the largest climb from reactants to the top.
S starts at 90 kJ, so its climb is only 60 kJ/mol. The climb, not the height, is Ea.
Releasing energy is about ΔH; Q's climb is just 40 kJ/mol.

why.correct: ΔH(P) = 110 − 50 = +60 kJ/mol; ΔH(Q) = 20 − 80 = −60 kJ/mol. Equal sizes, opposite directions of energy flow.
options: Same size, but P's products are higher than its reactants, so P absorbs energy.
Every hump is above its reactants; the hump sets Ea, while the end points set ΔH.
Right: P ends 60 kJ higher (+60) and Q ends 60 kJ lower (−60).
Ea and ΔH are separate: P climbs 95 kJ/mol and Q climbs 40 kJ/mol.

why.correct: Ea(reverse) = top of the hump − products = 160 kJ − 95 kJ = 65 kJ/mol.
Energies on the diagram are vertical differences. The difference between the two flat ends is ΔH.
options: Right: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants).
That distance is the forward activation energy.
The horizontal axis shows progress of the reaction, not energy.
The peak's height alone is neither ΔH nor Ea; energies are differences between levels.

why.correct: The diagram shows the system. An exothermic system ends with less enthalpy, so the products sit below the reactants.
options: Atoms are conserved, but energy is not stored the same way in different bonds; the levels differ.
Right: warming the solution means the system lost energy, so ΔH < 0 and the products sit lower.
The surroundings gain energy; the system, whose enthalpy is drawn, loses it.
The student's hump is not the issue, and exothermic reactions do have activation energies.

why.correct: Two separate readings: the end levels give the sign of ΔH; the hump gives the activation energy, which governs speed (5.6).
options: A small hump fits a fast reaction, but products below reactants make it exothermic.
Endothermic is right, but a tall hump means a large Ea and a slow reaction.
Right: products above reactants means endothermic; a small hump means a small Ea and a fast reaction.
Level ends give ΔH = 0, and a reaction that rearranges bonds has a hump.

why.correct: Reading a diagram backward: same levels, same hump; ΔH flips sign, and Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH = 70 − (−45) = 115 kJ/mol.

variables.name: Size of ΔH
variables.why: The same two levels are compared, so the size, 45 kJ/mol, is unchanged; only the sign flips.

variables.name: Activation energy
variables.why: The reverse climb starts from the lower product level: 70 + 45 = 115 kJ/mol.

variables.name: Enthalpy of the starting substances
variables.why: The reverse reaction starts at the products, which sit 45 kJ lower than the forward reactants.

why.correct: ΔH (end levels) tells how much energy is released; Ea (the hump) tells whether molecules have enough energy to start. Once burning, the energy released keeps lighting new molecules.
options: Right: the low products make it strongly exothermic; the hump (Ea) is why it needs a start.
A ΔH of −890 kJ/mol means the products are far below the reactants.
Without a hump, methane would burn the moment it met air; the spark is needed.
Level ends would mean ΔH = 0, not −890 kJ/mol.

why.correct: An energy diagram gives enthalpy levels: the sign and size of ΔH and both activation energies. For an exothermic reaction, the reverse Ea is the larger one.
options: Temperature is not on the diagram; its axes are enthalpy and progress of the reaction.
Right: both follow from where the ends sit relative to each other and to the hump.
The diagram gives Ea but not a rate constant or a time; those need more data.
Masses come from stoichiometry, not from an energy diagram.

why.correct: Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH. With ΔH negative, Ea(reverse) is larger.
options: That is true for an endothermic reaction, where the reactants are lower.
Same hump, different starting levels, so different climbs.
Right: the reverse climb starts from the lower product level, so it is longer by |ΔH|.
The reverse still has to climb the hump; its Ea is the larger of the two.

why.correct: Thermal equilibrium means equal temperatures, so no net energy flows. Both read 29.4 °C from 240 s onward.
options: Right: from 240 s on, both curves are flat at the same temperature.
At 0 s the temperatures differ by 74 °C, so energy is flowing fast.
At 90 s the block is still 1.8 °C warmer than the water, so energy still flows.
At 120 s the block (29.9 °C) is still warmer than the water (29.4 °C).

why.correct: Energy transfer is fastest when the temperature difference is largest, here at the start (74.0 °C apart at 0 s); it slows as the temperatures approach each other.
options: Cold does not flow. Energy flows from the block to the water.
Right: the larger the gap, the larger the difference in particle speeds at the boundary and the faster energy moves.
The rate depends on the temperature difference between the two objects, not on the block alone.
The block was removed from the heat at 0 s; its temperature only falls.

why.correct: Energy is conserved: q(lost by block) = q(gained by water). A temperature change depends on the energy and on what absorbs it; the same energy warms 200 g of water by far fewer degrees than it cools 120 g of aluminum.
options: In an insulated container, energy lost by the block equals energy gained by the water.
The container is insulated; the water's energy came from the block.
Right: equal energy, different temperature changes. The 200 g of water needs far more energy per degree than the 120 g block does.
Energy is conserved: it moves but is not destroyed.

why.correct: Energy is conserved in an insulated container: energy gained by the water = energy lost by the block = 7.06 kJ.
Temperature is set by the average kinetic energy of the particles. The longer motion lines in A show faster particles, so A is hotter.
options: Right: temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles, and A's are faster.
Slower particles have less kinetic energy, so B is cooler.
The number of particles does not set temperature; their average speed does.
The side that receives energy is the cooler one, which is B.

why.correct: Heat transfer is energy passed by collisions: A's fast particles speed up the wall's atoms, and those speed up B's particles.
options: The key says the wall stops particles; only energy gets through.
Right: energy passes collision by collision, from faster particles to slower ones, through the wall's atoms.
There is no flow of cold. Energy flows from A to B.
The wall passes energy along; it does not add its own.

why.correct: Energy flows from A to B until both have the same average kinetic energy (the same temperature). Particles and total energy are conserved.

variables.name: Average speed of the particles of A
variables.why: Gas A loses energy through the wall, so its particles slow down.

variables.name: Average speed of the particles of B
variables.why: Gas B gains that energy, so its particles speed up.

variables.name: Number of particles in each chamber
variables.why: The wall lets energy through but not particles.

variables.name: Total energy of the two gases together
variables.why: The chambers are insulated, so the energy lost by A equals the energy gained by B.

why.correct: At thermal equilibrium the average kinetic energies match. Individual collisions still pass energy, but as much goes each way, so the net flow is zero.
options: Particles keep a spread of speeds; it is the average that becomes equal.
Particles keep moving and colliding at any temperature above absolute zero.
At equal temperatures there is no net flow in either direction.
Right: equilibrium is dynamic. Collisions continue; there is just no net flow of energy.

why.correct: Energy moves by collisions from the hotter tea to the cooler spoon. The spoon warms, the tea cools a little, and both end at one temperature between 22 °C and 80 °C.
options: Right: energy flows from the warmer object to the cooler one until thermal equilibrium.
Only energy moves; the tea cools because it loses energy to the spoon.
Energy flows from hot to cold, and the final temperature is between 22 °C and 80 °C.
Any two objects in contact at different temperatures exchange energy.

why.correct: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Objects contain thermal energy; they exchange heat.
options: That is thermal energy. Heat is the energy that moves from one object to another.
Right: heat is energy in transit, not something an object contains.
That describes temperature (average kinetic energy).
Heat is not a substance; it is energy passed by particle collisions.

why.correct: Touch senses how fast your skin loses energy, not the object's temperature. Metal conducts energy away faster.
options: Both have been outside all night at the same temperature.
Nothing gives off cold; energy moves from your hand into the bench.
Right: both are at 2 °C, but metal carries energy away from your warmer skin more quickly, so your skin cools faster.
The wood is colder than your skin, so it also takes energy from you, just more slowly.

why.correct: Energy lost by the block = energy gained by the water = 1.85 kJ × 1000 J/kJ = 1.85 × 10³ J (1850 J, three significant figures).
Energy lost by the hot water equals energy gained by the cold water. With equal masses of the same substance, each changes by the same number of degrees, 20 °C, to meet at 40 °C.
options: Right: equal masses of the same substance, so the hot water loses as many degrees as the cold water gains: 60 − 20 = 40, split evenly.
Temperatures do not add. Energy flows from the hot water to the cold water until they meet in between.
The cold water cannot stay at 20 °C while energy flows into it.
The hot water loses energy, so it cannot stay at 60 °C.

why.correct: The final temperature lies between the two starting temperatures. With equal masses of the same material it is the average, (90 + 30) / 2 = 60 °C.
options: The block receives energy, so it must warm above 30 °C.
Right: same substance, same mass, so the hot one drops as much as the cold one rises, meeting halfway.
The nail loses energy, so it must cool below 90 °C.
A final temperature below both starting values would need energy to leave the insulated box.

why.correct: Energy flows from the warmer drink to the cooler ice through collisions. The drink's particles slow down, so its temperature falls.
options: Slowness is not passed along; energy is, from the faster particles to the slower ones.
Particles are not removed; the drink loses energy, not matter.
Right: energy moves from the drink into the ice, slowing the drink's particles.
The main flow is from the drink into the ice, which is in contact with it.

why.correct: Thermal equilibrium means equal temperature, which means equal average kinetic energy and no net energy transfer.
options: A bathtub and a cup can be at the same temperature with very different amounts of thermal energy.
Any two substances can reach the same temperature.
Particle mass does not matter; average kinetic energy does.
Right: equal temperatures mean energy passes equally both ways.

why.correct: 50.0 mL × (1 L / 1000 mL) × 1.00 mol/L = 0.0500 mol of H⁺, and the same amount of OH⁻. They react 1 : 1, so 0.0500 mol of H₂O forms.

The solution gained 2.788 kJ, so the reaction released it: q(reaction) = −2.788 kJ. ΔH = −2.788 kJ / 0.0500 mol = −55.76 kJ/mol → −55.8 kJ/mol. The sign is negative because the reaction is exothermic.

The calculation assumes every joule released warms the solution. Losses to the room lower the highest temperature, so the calculated q and |ΔH| come out too small: ΔH is less negative than the true value.
options: The reaction releases the same energy per mole; less of it is caught by the solution.
The same energy is released, but less is measured; the calculation uses the measured ΔT.
The reaction is still exothermic. Only the size of the calculated value changes.
Right: energy lost to the room never shows up as a temperature rise, so q looks smaller and so does |ΔH|.

why.correct: q doubles (twice the moles react) and m doubles, so ΔT = q / (m c) is unchanged. ΔH per mole is q / n, and both double, so it is unchanged too.
options: Right: twice the energy is released into twice the mass of solution, so ΔT and the per-mole value do not change.
Twice the energy goes into twice the mass, so each gram warms by the same amount.
ΔH per mole is a property of the reaction; it does not change with the amount used.
There is twice as much reaction as well as twice as much solution, so the rise stays the same.

why.correct: ΔT = T(lowest) − T(start) = 19.04 − 22.40 = −3.36 °C. The lowest point is where the dissolving stops absorbing energy.
options: The slow rise after 150 s is energy leaking in from the room, not part of the dissolving.
Right: the lowest temperature marks the end of the dissolving; after that, the room warms the cup.
That is a temperature, not a change. ΔT = final − initial.
The temperature keeps falling until about 150 s, when the dissolving is complete.

why.correct: n = 5.35 g ÷ 53.49 g/mol = 0.1000 mol. The solution lost 1.480 kJ, so the dissolving absorbed it: q = +1.480 kJ. ΔH = +1.480 kJ ÷ 0.1000 mol = +14.79 → +14.8 kJ/mol.
q(dissolving) = −q(solution). The solution's temperature fell, so q(solution) < 0 and q(dissolving) > 0: endothermic.
options: Right: the solution lost energy (negative) and the dissolving gained the same energy (positive).
This would fit a temperature rise. Here the solution cooled.
Energy lost by one is gained by the other, so the signs are opposite.
Transfer means one side loses (negative) and one side gains (positive).

why.correct: A foam cup slows energy exchange but does not stop it. A solution colder than the room slowly gains energy, which is why the lowest point, not the last reading, gives ΔT.
options: Dissolving does not reverse by itself while the salt stays in solution.
Right: once the dissolving is done, the solution is colder than the room, so energy flows in.
Dissolving NH₄Cl absorbs energy, so faster dissolving would cool the solution.
The thermometer is at the solution's temperature; the rise comes from outside the cup.

why.correct: Specific heat capacity, c, is the energy needed to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K, the same size step).
options: Specific heat is per gram. Per mole would be about 75.3 J/(mol·°C).
Specific heat describes a change in temperature, not an amount of energy at one temperature.
Right: specific heat is the energy per gram per degree.
Specific heat applies while the temperature changes, not to boiling.

why.correct: For equal energy per gram, ΔT is inversely related to c. Water's specific heat, 4.18 J/(g·°C), is about five times that of sand, so water warms far less.
options: A higher specific heat would mean a smaller temperature rise, not a larger one.
Right: ΔT = q / (m c); a smaller c means a larger ΔT for the same energy per gram.
Both absorb energy; the same energy changes the water's temperature less.
Particle size does not set this; the energy needed per gram per degree does.

why.correct: Heat capacity, C = m × c, is the energy to warm a whole object by 1 °C. A swimming pool and a cup of water have the same specific heat but very different heat capacities.
options: They differ by the mass: one is per gram, the other for the whole object.
This swaps them. "Specific" means per gram.
Right: heat capacity = mass × specific heat.
Both describe energy per degree; neither is just J or just °C.

why.correct: Water: 150.0 g × 4.18 J/(g·°C) × 6.16 °C = 3862.3 J. Calorimeter: 32.5 J/°C × 6.16 °C = 200.2 J. Total = 4062.5 J = 4.06 kJ released by the reaction.
Moles of water = moles of the limiting reactant, NaOH: 0.0250 L × 1.00 mol/L = 0.0250 mol. ΔH = −1.39 kJ ÷ 0.0250 mol = −55.6 kJ/mol.
options: Right: NaOH (0.0250 mol) is the limiting reactant, so 0.0250 mol of water forms: −1.39 kJ / 0.0250 mol = −55.6 kJ/mol.
HCl is in excess; half of it does not react. Divide by the moles that actually react.
Adding the moles of both reactants double-counts each reaction event and includes excess acid.
The solution gained energy, so the reaction lost it: ΔH is negative.

why.correct: Anything that makes the measured q too small, or the moles used in the division too large, makes the calculated ΔH less negative.
options: Lost energy does not raise the temperature, so the measured q is too small.
ΔT is too small, so q is too small.
A larger m makes the calculated q larger, so ΔH comes out more negative.
Dividing the same q by fewer moles makes |ΔH| larger, more negative.
A lower starting value makes ΔT larger, so |ΔH| comes out larger.
Less reacts, so less energy is released, but the calculation still divides by the full amount.

why.correct: Energy released depends on the moles that react; ΔT depends on that energy and the mass it warms; ΔH per mole depends only on the reaction.

variables.name: Energy released by the reaction
variables.why: The same moles react, so the same energy is released.

variables.name: Temperature rise of the solution
variables.why: The same energy spreads through twice the mass, so ΔT is about half.

variables.name: Calculated ΔH per mole of limiting reactant
variables.why: q = m c ΔT is the same (twice m, half ΔT) and so are the moles, so ΔH is unchanged.

why.correct: Energy lost by hot water = energy gained by cold water: 50.0 × 4.18 × (80.0 − T) = 100.0 × 4.18 × (T − 20.0). So 4000 − 50.0 T = 100.0 T − 2000, 150.0 T = 6000, T = 40.0 °C.
Sloped parts show one phase warming; flat parts show two phases changing at constant temperature. The liquid alone is the slope between the two flat parts.
options: Right: melting has finished at the end of the first flat part, and boiling has not yet begun.
This flat part is melting: solid and liquid are both present.
This flat part is boiling: liquid and gas are both present.
Before the first flat part, the sample is a solid warming up.

why.correct: Melting time = 47.2 s − 9.6 s = 37.6 s. Energy = 37.6 s × 150. J/s = 5640 J = 5.64 kJ. Moles = 47.05 g ÷ 94.10 g/mol = 0.500 mol. ΔHfus = 5.64 kJ ÷ 0.500 mol = 11.28 → 11.3 kJ/mol.
Melting turns a fixed arrangement into a liquid where molecules still touch; vaporizing pulls them apart into a gas. More attractions are overcome, so ΔHvap > ΔHfus.
options: No covalent bonds break in either change; the molecules are still Compound Q in the gas.
The plateau length measures energy to overcome attractions, not the temperature.
Right: in the liquid, molecules still touch and attract; boiling overcomes nearly all those attractions.
The same 0.500 mol of Compound Q melts and then boils.

why.correct: Temperature tracks average kinetic energy. On a flat part, the added energy separates molecules (potential energy goes up) while their average speed stays constant.
options: The energy is added, but it does not speed the molecules up while the temperature is flat.
Spreading out raises their potential energy; their average speed stays the same at constant temperature.
No covalent bonds break, and breaking bonds would absorb energy, not release it.
Right: constant temperature means constant average kinetic energy; the energy raises the potential energy.

why.correct: ΔHvap measures the energy to separate molecules. With similar masses, the type of attraction decides: hydrogen bonding (water) ≫ London dispersion only (methane).
options: The molar masses (18.02 and 16.04 g/mol) are nearly the same, so mass cannot explain a fivefold difference.
